title: 5 Signs You've Lost Control Of Your Class (But Don't Know It)
author: Michael Linsin
summary: After coaching hundreds of teachers, Linsin identifies a recurring pattern: many teachers who have effectively lost control of their class don't realize it because they've grown so accustomed to disorder that it no longer registers as abnormal. He lists five diagnostic signs—talking over students, having to repeat and remind constantly, a strained or argumentative relationship with students, working harder than the students themselves, and struggling to get the class's attention—each of which he explains as evidence of a specific breakdown in teacher influence and leadership. He argues that accepting chronic stress and disrespect as simply "part of the job" is a lie many teachers unconsciously buy into. His remedy is straightforward: recognize the signs, gather the courage to abandon the current approach entirely, and start over with a genuinely followed classroom management plan.
points: Many teachers who have lost control of their class don't recognize it because chronic disorder has become normalized to them.
Talking over students while giving instruction is identified as clear evidence of lost teacher influence.
Constant reminding and repeating trains students to tune the teacher out entirely.
Working harder than the students signals an imbalance where the burden of learning has shifted away from them.
The belief that stress and disrespect are simply part of the teaching job is called a lie that keeps teachers from starting over.
quotes: It’s the scores of teachers who have lost control of their class but continue to plow forward.
Well, after coaching hundreds of teachers over the past couple of years, and asking this very question, I now know the answer: It’s because they don’t realize they’ve lost control.

If you feel you have no choice but to give instruction while your students are talking (because of the time and trouble it takes to get them quiet), then you have very little influence over their behavior.
If you find yourself repeating much of what you say, and reminding your students again and again about the same things, then you’ve effectively trained them to tune you out.
In well-run, well-behaved classrooms, the teacher focuses on delivering great lessons while the burden of listening and learning falls in toto onto the shoulders of students.
The notion that stress and frustration are just part of the job is a lie.
